result: Midnight draped its velvet shawl over the quiet town, and somewhere beneath the dull orange halo of a streetlamp, I discovered a small spiral notebook abandoned on a bench. The cover was cracked and rain-speckled, but when I opened it the pages were startlingly dry, as though the paper had trained itself to shrug off weather just to guard the words inside. I sat, breath visible, listening to the faint hum of sodium lights, and began to read. Inside, someone had been cataloging dreams in hurried graphite loops: a desert that became an ocean without anyone noticing, a library where books whispered each other's endings, a train that moved backward through the calendar until passengers met their childhood selves. The handwriting leaned forward impatiently, as if the author feared waking before finishing the sentence. I still don’t know why I took the notebook home, but I did, sliding it into my coat like contraband inspiration. That night I placed it beside my pillow and promised myself I would return it if the town posted flyers, but weeks passed in silence. Instead the notebook began to colonize my routine. Each morning I found a new entry even though I had not written anything, as if the dreams were drafting themselves the moment I blinked. One described a forest knit from clock hands, every branch ticking toward some unseen hour. Another traced the outline of a door painted on the underside of a river, a door fish could swim through but humans could not touch. I tried staying awake, pen in hand, daring the pages to move while I watched, yet sometime between two and three a.m. I always slipped, and the next morning the notebook would greet me with fresh, impossible ink. Eventually I began to answer. If the dream wrote of a question, I scribbled a reply; when it narrated a place, I added directions, landmarks, weather patterns, anything to prove I had been listening. Soon the entries resembled conversations, two voices threading between lines, though I could never decide which was mine. The notebook taught me new alphabets composed of negative space, glyphs shaped like the holes left after birds migrate. It recorded the sound of moss breathing, the precise shade of green grief turns after a year, the equation for silence when multiplied by distance. I filled marginalia with coffee stains and fingerprints like co-signatures. Days lost their edges. Work meetings felt dubbed from another language, friends seemed to flicker like low-battery holograms, and street signs occasionally rearranged themselves into anagrams when I passed. Reality, I realized, is only a consensus draft, and I was editing mine with every nocturnal annotation. Then came the night the notebook left me an address. No story, no riddles, only coordinates penciled with uncharacteristic neatness, followed by a time: 3:33 A.M. I felt like a character finally summoned off the margins. So I brewed midnight coffee, dressed in layers, and walked. The streets were lacquered with moonlight and frost, silent except for my own pulse humming behind my ears. Following the coordinates, I arrived at the old train station long abandoned since the rail company digitized its routes. Windows were boarded, but lamplight leaked through cracks as if someone were rehearsing dawn inside. The door, impossibly, swung when I touched it. A warm gust smelled of cedar and photocopied paper. Inside, the station had been converted into a library of moments. Shelves stood where tracks once ran, and on those shelves rested jars, each holding what looked like a memory distilled into color and motion. One jar glowed with the soft blue of first love; another shimmered like the iridescent tail of a comet breaking up in atmosphere. Each was labeled in handwriting that mirrored the notebook’s, but the author had signed nothing. As I wandered, I noticed an empty shelf, a lone space waiting. Beside it rested a placard: “Contribution Due”. And suddenly I understood—the notebook had been interviewing me, coaxing experiences worth bottling. My pockets held nothing but keys, but my head was brimming. I thought of the clock-hand forest, the river door, the negative alphabet, and realized they were now mine to give. So I opened the notebook one last time. Its pages were blank. I set it on the shelf, spine outward, aligning it with the invisible geometry of the place. Instantly the notebook dissolved into light, condensed, and became a jar sealed with my initials. Inside swirled a forest of ticking branches beneath a paper sky. I swear I heard the color green exhale. When I turned, a figure stood by the door—a woman holding a pen that glowed like phosphorus. She nodded, neither welcoming nor dismissing, merely acknowledging that the exchange was complete. I left without speaking, carrying nothing, yet feeling several ounces lighter, as though part of my gravity had been filed under Reference. Outside, dawn finally yawned over the horizon, peeling back the stars like stickers. The streetlamps clicked off in sequence, and morning commuters would soon rewrite the town’s ordinary narrative. I wondered how many of them were secretly authors of jars they'd never see. Weeks have passed since then, and though I sometimes wake with sentences itching behind my eyelids, no new notebook has appeared. I keep waiting, unsure whether silence is permission or conclusion. In the meantime, I have started carrying blank index cards, just in case a stray dream needs somewhere to land. Sometimes I leave one on a bus seat, sometimes under a coffee cup, sometimes folded into a library book already overdue. I like to think the cards migrate, collecting scribbles, forming flocks of unfinished possibility. Maybe one night they will roost inside an abandoned station, and someone else will follow coordinates to find a shelf waiting. If they do, I hope they bring an extra word for me.
